description: Cognitive neuroscience, CT/PET/fMRI scanning, Tulving's gold memory study, and stroke.
content_html:
What Is Cognitive Neuroscience?

Cognitive neuroscience is a field of study that bridges biology and psychology. It asks: how do physical structures in the brain produce thoughts, memories and behaviours? Thanks to advances in brain scanning technology, researchers can observe the living brain in action and link patterns of neural activity to specific psychological functions.

Brain Scanning Techniques

Before modern scanning, the only way to study the brain was through case studies of people with brain injuries or through post-mortem examination. Today, three main scanning methods allow researchers to study the brain non-invasively.

A CT scan (Computed Tomography) uses a series of X-rays from different angles to create detailed cross-sectional images of the brain’s structure. CT scans are fast and widely available, making them useful in medical emergencies such as identifying a stroke or a tumour. However, they show structure only — not which areas are active.

A PET scan (Positron Emission Tomography) works differently. The patient is injected with a small amount of radioactive glucose. As the brain uses glucose for energy, the most active areas absorb the most glucose and produce the most radioactive emissions. The scanner detects these emissions and creates a colour-coded map showing brain activity. PET scans show function, but the resolution is lower than MRI and the participant must be injected with a radioactive substance.

An fMRI scan (Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging) detects changes in blood oxygenation. When a brain area is active, it receives more oxygenated blood. The fMRI detects this and produces detailed, real-time images of which areas are working during a given task. fMRI has high spatial resolution, involves no radiation, and is currently the most widely used technique in cognitive neuroscience research.

Key Fact

Three scanning techniques: CT (X-rays, structure only, fast), PET (radioactive tracer, shows activity, lower resolution), fMRI (blood oxygen, real-time activity, high resolution, no radiation). CT and PET are older; fMRI is currently the most precise for research.

Aim: Endel Tulving aimed to use brain scanning to investigate whether episodic memory (personal memories) and semantic memory (general knowledge) are stored in different areas of the brain.

Method: Tulving used PET scanning while participants recalled either episodic memories (personal, experienced events) or semantic memories (general facts). He observed which brain areas showed increased activity during each type of recall.

Results: Episodic memory recall was associated with greater activity in the right prefrontal cortex, while semantic memory recall was associated with greater activity in the left prefrontal cortex. This pattern was consistent across participants.

Conclusion: The two types of long-term memory are supported by different, lateralised brain regions. This was important evidence that memory is not a single, unified function but is neurologically divided — supporting the idea of distinct memory systems and the principle of localisation of function.

Key Fact

Tulving’s gold memory study used PET scans to show that episodic memory recall activates the right prefrontal cortex and semantic memory recall activates the left prefrontal cortex — demonstrating that different memory types are neurologically distinct.

Neurological Damage: Stroke and Injury

Understanding what happens when the brain is damaged provides powerful evidence for localisation of function. A stroke occurs when the blood supply to part of the brain is cut off, causing neurons in that region to die due to oxygen deprivation. Because neurons cannot regenerate, the damage is often permanent.

The effects of a stroke depend entirely on which area of the brain is affected. A stroke in the motor cortex may cause paralysis or weakness on one side of the body (the opposite side to the damage, because the brain’s motor pathways cross over). A stroke affecting Broca’s area in the left frontal lobe may cause difficulty producing speech, while a stroke affecting Wernicke’s area in the temporal lobe may disrupt language comprehension.

A strength of brain scanning is that it provides objective, non-invasive evidence about brain function in living people, moving beyond the limitations of post-mortem case studies. This has greatly expanded our understanding of where psychological functions are located.

However, brain scans have weaknesses. They show correlation, not causation — an area lighting up during a task does not prove that area causes that function. Scans also measure activity across thousands of neurons at once, so fine-grained detail is limited. PET scans involve radioactive tracers, raising ethical concerns about exposing participants to radiation. All scans also require participants to lie still in an artificial laboratory setting, which may not reflect real-world brain activity.
exam_tip_html: When comparing scanning techniques, use a table in your notes: CT (structure, X-rays, fast), PET (activity, radioactive tracer, colour map), fMRI (activity, blood oxygen, real-time, high resolution). In an exam, if asked to “evaluate” a scanning technique, always state a strength AND a weakness and develop each with a reason. For Tulving’s study, remember the result in lateralisation terms: right = episodic, left = semantic.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Cognitive neuroscience investigates how brain structure and activity relate to behaviour. CT scans show brain structure; PET and fMRI show activity — with fMRI offering the best resolution and no radiation.
  • Tulving used PET scans to show that episodic memory (right prefrontal cortex) and semantic memory (left prefrontal cortex) are neurologically distinct.
  • Neurological damage, such as a stroke, destroys neurons in the affected area, producing predictable effects on behaviour that depend on which region is damaged — providing real-world evidence for localisation of function.

practice_questions.text:
Which scanning technique detects changes in blood oxygen levels to produce real-time images of brain activity?
A) CT scan
B) PET scan
C) fMRI scan

practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise definition stating it is the study of how brain structure and/or function relates to cognitive processes such as memory, perception or behaviour — both elements present [2 marks].
Secure: Links the brain to mental processes but does not specify what type of brain information (structure/function) or the type of mental process [1 mark].
Developing: Vague reference to how the brain relates to thinking [0–1 mark].
Emerging: Incorrect or irrelevant [0 marks].

practice_questions.text: Describe how a PET scan works.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per accurate point up to 3 marks. Students may include: the patient is injected with a radioactive substance (often glucose); the most active brain areas use the most glucose and emit the most radioactivity; the scanner detects these emissions and creates a colour-coded map of brain activity.
Mastering: All three steps described in sequence, using accurate terms.
Secure: Two steps described.
Developing: States the scan shows activity but without explaining the mechanism.
Emerging: Vague mention of detecting the brain without any mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Explain how evidence from neurological damage, such as a stroke, supports the principle of localisation of function.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Defines stroke (blocked blood supply kills neurons in that region), identifies that effects depend on which region is damaged, provides a specific example (e.g. motor cortex damage → paralysis; Broca's area damage → speech production affected), and explicitly links this to localisation. Two developed, linked points.
Secure: Defines stroke and links damage in a specific area to a specific function loss.
Developing: States stroke damages the brain and causes problems, but without linking to specific areas and their functions.
Emerging: Vague reference to brain damage affecting behaviour.

practice_questions.text: Describe Tulving's 'gold' memory study, including the aim, method, results and conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each for: aim (to investigate whether episodic and semantic memory are supported by different brain areas); method (PET scanning while participants recalled episodic or semantic memories); results (episodic memory → right prefrontal cortex; semantic memory → left prefrontal cortex); conclusion (the two memory types are neurologically distinct/lateralised); significance (provides evidence for both different memory systems and localisation of function).
Mastering: All five points accurately described.
Secure: Four points.
Developing: Two or three.
Emerging: Vague reference to Tulving studying memory with a scan, no AMRC structure.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the use of brain scanning techniques to investigate brain function.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate descriptions of all three techniques (CT, PET, fMRI) with the key difference between structural (CT) and functional (PET/fMRI) scans; reference to Tulving's study as an example of PET use; two elaborated evaluative points (e.g. objective, non-invasive evidence from living participants — strength; correlation not causation, artificial setting — weaknesses), each developed with a reason.
Secure: Two techniques described accurately; two evaluative points with some development.
Developing: One or two techniques described; one evaluative point.
Emerging: Mentions scanning without accurate description; evaluation is a single unsupported statement.
[AO1 ~4 marks; AO3 ~5 marks]

A stroke occurs when the blood supply to part of the brain is blocked, causing the neurons in that region to _____ due to oxygen deprivation.
Tulving used _____ scans to compare brain activity during episodic and semantic memory recall.

right: Brain activity via blood oxygen levels

flashcard_questions.a: How brain structure and function relate to cognitive processes like memory and perception.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a CT scan detect, and what technique does it use?
flashcard_questions.a: Brain structure, using X-rays to create cross-sectional images.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a PET scan detect?
flashcard_questions.a: Brain activity, by tracking a radioactive tracer absorbed by active neurons.

flashcard_questions.q: What does an fMRI scan detect, and what is its main advantage over PET?
flashcard_questions.a: Brain activity via blood oxygen levels; higher resolution and no radiation.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the aim of Tulving's gold memory study?
flashcard_questions.a: To find out whether episodic and semantic memory activate different brain areas.

Which brain region was active during semantic memory recall in Tulving's study?
What did Tulving conclude about episodic and semantic memory?
flashcard_questions.a: They are neurologically distinct — supported by different, lateralised brain areas.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a stroke, and why is its damage often permanent?
flashcard_questions.a: A stroke is a blocked blood supply to part of the brain; neurons die and cannot regenerate.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one strength of using brain scanning to study behaviour.
flashcard_questions.a: It provides objective, non-invasive evidence from living participants.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one weakness of brain scanning research.
flashcard_questions.a: Scans show correlation not causation — activity does not prove that area causes the function.

glossary_terms.definition: The scientific study of how brain structure and function relate to cognitive processes such as memory, attention, language and perception.
Computed Tomography — a scanning technique that uses X-rays to produce detailed cross-sectional images of brain structure.
Positron Emission Tomography — a scanning technique that detects radioactive tracers in the blood to show which areas of the brain are most active.
Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging — a scanning technique that detects changes in blood oxygen levels to produce real-time images of brain activity.
A medical event in which blood supply to part of the brain is blocked or a blood vessel bursts, causing cells in that area to die.
